case_study_insert.main_stem: Nordic Precision Bearings (NPB) is a worker cooperative in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2007 by Anders Nord, it manufactures sealed ball bearings for wind turbines and machine tools and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. NPB plans to invest $880,000 in a robotic bearing-grinding line, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $400,000 of member share capital. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. NPB faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 2.6% in grinding and rising waste of steel alloy, with delivery times lengthening.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The grinding line finished 23,200 bearings last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 3.9% a year earlier. Alloy waste fell from 41 to 28 tonnes a month, while average delivery time stretched from 3.4 to 5.1 days. A survey of 470 equipment buyers found 59% would pay up to $0.45 more for sealed long-life bearings and 51% check supplier reliability before ordering. Records show 11 of 48 members have not completed on-the-job training on the grinding robots; robotics courses cost $710 per employee.
case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.1% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $13.10 to $13.78 an hour from April 2026. (3) Bearing-steel and alloy input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, freight and energy inflation is 4.9%, while wind-turbine component demand grew 3.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: NPB plans to raise $480,000 through a bank loan for its $880,000 grinding line. Explain two disadvantages for NPB of using a bank loan rather than member share capital.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bank loan requires interest and capital repayments, so at a base rate raised to 4.9% the $480,000 borrowing adds a fixed financial burden on top of $288,000 a year operating costs. That drains cash which could otherwise cover the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 bearings and fund on-the-job training for the 11 of 48 members still learning the grinding robots.

Point 2: Lenders commonly require collateral and impose conditions, which can reduce the autonomy of a worker cooperative and put its assets at risk if the 2.6% defect rate delays returns from the $880,000 line. Member share capital of $400,000 carries no such fixed claim and keeps decision-making inside the cooperative, whereas a lender may restrict further borrowing or demand priority repayment, limiting NPB's flexibility on quality investment and the $710 robotics courses.

Interest on the $480,000 loan would also compete with the $710 robotics courses needed for the 11 of 48 members still in training, so member share capital, despite diluting ownership, better fits a cooperative's long-term aims.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid disadvantage of a bank loan (max 2).
1 mark for each valid disadvantage of a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NPB's interest cost, training and contribution.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NPB's collateral, control and cooperative status.

questions.question_text: NPB is promoting its new sealed long-life bearings. Consider advertising in engineering trade journals, sponsoring a wind-energy exhibition, or e-commerce and digital marketing. Which should NPB choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Engineering trade journal advertising: Specialist bearing and machine-tool magazines reach the 470 surveyed equipment buyers' peers and can carry the $0.45 premium message accepted by 59%. Yet circulation is narrow, insertions must be repeated, and print cannot demonstrate the reliability checked by 51% of buyers, so returns are weak for a 48-member cooperative funding an $880,000 line.

Wind-energy exhibition sponsorship: A stand lets turbine makers inspect sealed bearings and ask about reliability, answering the 51% who check supplier track record and helping counter the 2.6% defect rate with visible samples. However, stand and travel costs are high, the event is brief and geographical, and it may not generate the steady demand needed to use 96,000 units of capacity.

E-commerce and digital marketing: A website can publish reliability data and specifications to the 51% who check them and promote the $0.45 long-life premium to the 59% who value it, at low cost per contact and with measurable enquiries. Results build gradually and require digital skills the cooperative may need to buy in, but campaigns can be scaled as the 5.1-day delivery issue is resolved.

Recommendation: NPB should choose e-commerce and digital marketing. It reaches the surveyed reliability-focused segment cost-effectively and can be tracked against 96,000-unit output. Trade journals are rejected as narrow and unmeasurable; the exhibition is rejected as expensive and short-lived. A small exhibition presence can be added later if online demand proves strong.

NPB should check that any online campaign converts into orders before the 5.1-day delivery time worsens further, since the 470 surveyed buyers value reliability and a poor fulfilment record would waste the $0.45 premium opportunity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to NPB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NPB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of NPB and recommends e-commerce, explaining why trade journals and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: NPB's 2.6% defect rate and lengthening delivery times are a concern. Explain two benefits for NPB of introducing job rotation in its grinding team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the 48 members between grinding stations, reducing boredom and repetitive strain while broadening skills — a form of job enrichment consistent with Herzberg. Fresh eyes on the 23,200 bearings finished last quarter can spot the causes of the 2.6% defect rate, and rotated staff can cover for the 11 of 48 members still needing on-the-job training, easing the 5.1-day delivery problem.

Point 2: Rotation spreads the $710 robotics courses across more members, so several people can operate the new grinding line and NPB is not dependent on a few specialists under laissez-faire leadership. Multi-skilling raises flexibility and morale in a worker cooperative, protecting the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units and helping cut the 41 tonnes of alloy waste a month recorded in the operations log.

The cooperative should rotate members on a fixed weekly schedule so everyone keeping the 23,200 bearings on specification gains experience, and it should record who has completed the $710 robotics course to keep the 5.1-day delivery target realistic.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of job rotation (max 2).
1 mark for each valid benefit of job rotation (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to NPB's defect rate, training and deliveries.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to NPB's multi-skilling, waste and contribution.

questions.question_text: NPB must improve quality on its new grinding robots. Consider quality control inspection or quality assurance. Which should NPB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control inspection: Checking finished bearings at the end of the line can catch the 2.6% defect rate before they reach wind-turbine clients and is simple to introduce with the 23,200 bearings made last quarter. However, inspection finds faults only after alloy and labour have been used, so the 41 tonnes of waste a month continue, and it does not prevent the 5.1-day delivery delays caused by rework.

Quality assurance: Building quality into each grinding stage through prevention, worker involvement and the $710 robotics courses for the 11 of 48 members still training addresses the cause of defects and cuts waste from 41 to 28 tonnes. It suits a worker cooperative where members can own quality, but it takes longer to embed and needs on-the-job training before results appear.

Decision: NPB should choose quality assurance as its main approach. Prevention removes the root cause of the 2.6% defect rate and reduces waste, protecting the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units. Pure inspection is rejected because it detects but does not stop defects and leaves rework delaying the 5.1-day deliveries; NPB should keep limited final sampling as a safety net while prevention becomes established.

NPB should begin with a small pilot on the grinding robots, recording defect counts on the 23,200 bearings before and after prevention measures, and use the $710 courses for the 11 of 48 members still training. Members should be rewarded for suggesting improvements, which fits the cooperative tradition and keeps waste falling from 41 to 28 tonnes. Only once defects are sustainably lower should routine final inspection be reduced, otherwise the 5.1-day delivery record could suffer and the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units be put at risk.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes quality control and quality assurance with limited application to NPB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of NPB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both approaches in the context of NPB and makes a justified decision that rejects pure inspection, covering waste, prevention and training.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NPB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $288,000 ÷ ($12.00 − $6.00) = $288,000 ÷ $6.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.00 − $6.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NPB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even of 48,000 units with output of 96,000 units: the margin of safety is 48,000 units, showing the cushion if turbine demand dips.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to price the $0.45 long-life premium and judge whether the $710 robotics courses and $480,000 loan are affordable.
3. Check that $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units can service the $480,000 bank loan and the $288,000 fixed costs before further investment.
4. Track productivity of 96,000 ÷ 48 members = 2,000 units per worker and unit cost of $288,000 ÷ 96,000 + $6.00 = $9.00 to spot waste and the 8.7% alloy price rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety 48,000 units; long-life premium pricing; loan-service targets; and productivity of 2,000 units per worker with unit cost $9.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NPB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NPB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.05 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: In 2024 current assets were $130,000 inventories + $170,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $360,000, and $360,000 ÷ $220,000 current liabilities gives the 2024 measure. In 2025 the corresponding assets were $180,000 + $180,000 + $45,000 = $405,000, and $405,000 ÷ $250,000 gives the 2025 measure. For the stock-excluding measure the 2024 numerator is $360,000 − $130,000 = $230,000, and $230,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.05; in 2025 $405,000 − $180,000 = $225,000 and $225,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.90.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The broad coverage measure edged down from 1.64 to 1.62 as current liabilities rose from $220,000 to $250,000 and cash fell from $60,000 to $45,000. The stock-excluding measure fell more sharply, from 1.05 to 0.90, because inventories built up from $130,000 to $180,000; NPB is relying more on selling bearings from stock to meet short-term debts while servicing a $480,000 bank loan. Receivables have also risen to $180,000, so if equipment buyers pay late the position could worsen further.

Conclusion: NPB's financial position has not improved; it has deteriorated. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.64 to 1.62 and 1.05 to 0.90) fell, with the sharpest decline in the measure that excludes stock. NPB should run down excess inventory and tighten credit control before adding to its borrowing.

With $480,000 of bank-loan commitments, NPB should prioritise rebuilding its cash balance before further borrowing, because the current position leaves little room for a delay in receiving the $180,000 owed by customers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current and acid test measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion that NPB's position did not improve.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NPB of introducing computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) on its grinding line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: CAM can grind bearings to tighter, repeatable tolerances, cutting the 2.6% defect rate on the 23,200 bearings finished last quarter and protecting the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units. Consistent precision supports the $0.45 long-life premium wanted by 59% of buyers and the reliability checked by 51%, strengthening the return on the $880,000 line.

Disadvantage: CAM adds capital cost to the $880,000 already committed and raises fixed costs above $288,000 a year, pushing the 48,000-unit break-even higher if wind-turbine orders dip. The 11 of 48 members still awaiting on-the-job training may need $710 robotics courses, and automation could reduce the hands-on problem-solving that currently helps bring alloy waste down from 41 to 28 tonnes a month.

CAM should be introduced on one grinding station first so NPB can verify the 2.6% defect rate falls on the 23,200 bearings made each quarter before extending it. The 11 of 48 members still untrained should complete the $710 course beforehand, so automation supports rather than replaces the practical problem-solving that has already cut alloy waste from 41 to 28 tonnes a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of CAM.
1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of CAM.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NPB's defect rate, premium and contribution.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NPB's break-even, training and waste.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.9%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in bearing-steel input costs will affect NPB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.1% to 4.9%): NPB has a $480,000 bank loan, but the insert does not state whether it is variable-rate, so any direct figure is only an illustrative bound: a full 0.8 percentage-point rise on $480,000 is 0.008 × $480,000 = $3,840 a year. That is modest next to $288,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the effect is zero; higher rates may still slow wind-turbine investment.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $13.78 an hour): The cooperative employs 48 members and the rise lifts wage costs, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 48 members = 2,000 units per worker. A higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Bearing-steel cost inflation (8.7%): The $6.00 variable cost is not decomposed, so only a bound is possible — if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% it would add 0.087 × $6.00 = $0.522 a unit, or 96,000 × $0.522 = $50,112 a year. Even a partial rise raises the 48,000-unit break-even, though the $0.45 premium accepted by 59% of buyers offers some recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in bearing-steel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 96,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution needed to service the $880,000 grinding line. The interest effect is at most a bounded $3,840 and the wage effect depends on productivity, so neither matches the reach of material inflation.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NPB's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in the context of NPB and justifies why input-cost inflation has the greatest impact while the other two are smaller.
